name: Quit smoking / vaping

lead: Smoking is associated with a distinctive aged look: wrinkles, sagging and a dull complexion. Quitting is discussed as a way to avoid that.
The association is documented in observational research; no trial of quitting for appearance was found, and vaping has not been studied for facial aging.

paras: Smoking is proposed to reduce skin oxygen and antioxidants, narrow blood vessels, and break down collagen and elastin.
Quitting itself carries no appearance-specific risks in the sources reviewed; smoking is linked to many serious diseases.

lead: In looksmaxxing and skincare discussions, quitting smoking or vaping is cited as a way to avoid or slow smoking-related facial aging. 'Smoker's face' is the term for facial changes seen in many long-term smokers, including a pattern of wrinkles, sagging and a dull, yellowish or grayish complexion [1].

Medical sources attribute these changes to reduced oxygen and nutrient supply, breakdown of the skin's structural matrix, and oxidative stress [1]. No trials of quitting for appearance were found in the sources reviewed, and no studies of vaping and facial aging were found.
infobox: Slower facial aging, better skin tone
Observational, as summarised in encyclopedic sources

paras: Wikipedia describes smoker's face as the distinctive changes in many tobacco smokers: wrinkling, sagging, premature aging, a grayish tone and higher skin cancer risk, along with hair loss and oral effects such as gum disease and staining [1]. A study it cites, a 1985 BMJ article, found characteristic features in about 46% of current smokers and 8% of former smokers with a decade of smoking, and none in non-smokers [1].

The cited mechanisms include increased enzymes that break down the extracellular matrix (collagen, elastin and proteoglycans), reduced antioxidants such as vitamin C, narrowing of facial blood vessels by tobacco chemicals, and a build-up of free radicals leading to oxidative stress, considered a form of extrinsic aging [1].
No studies of vaping and facial appearance were found in the sources reviewed.
No studies found on quitting smoking or vaping with facial appearance as the outcome. The relevant evidence is observational research on smokers' skin, as summarised above [1].
